extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, communication scholars, and students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on integrating communication theories (e.g., systems theory, social learning, social exchange, coorientation, elaboration-likelihood) into the research, audience analysis, and writing of public relations materials; includes case studies and media-selection considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of theory/theory building as foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners should use theory and theory building as a foundation for understanding, researching, and writing about organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory should inform campaign design, audience analysis, and message construction; the paper examines the marriage of theory and practice of writing public relations materials for a client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply general systems theory to campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ general systems theory as a lens in public relations campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systems-thinking to analyze organizational-environment relationships and message flows; the paper discusses general systems theory and presents related case studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use information processing models to predict audience attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider information processing as a predictor of attitudes of target audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design messages and choose strategies informed by how target audiences process information, to influence attitudes effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply social learning theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate social learning theory into the analysis and crafting of PR messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper explains social learning theory and provides case studies illustrating its application to public relations writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply social exchange theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Use social exchange theory to inform PR strategy and messaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reciprocity, costs/benefits, and relationship dynamics when composing and evaluating PR communications; case studies are presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply symmetrical communication theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Use symmetrical communication theory (two-way, balanced communication) as a standard for PR practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design communications that support mutual understanding and balanced exchanges between organization and publics; discussed with examples in the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use coorientation model to identify publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the coorientation model to correctly identify and understand publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coorientation (comparing organization and public perceptions) helps determine shared and divergent views; the paper discusses this model alongside case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use elaboration-likelihood model (ELM) for public identification and message design
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ the elaboration-likelihood theory to explain how publics are identified and how messages persuade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use central vs. peripheral processing distinctions to tailor messages to audience motivation and ability; the paper includes case studies applying ELM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the right medium based on theoretical and audience considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Select media channels for PR messages using a series of considerations informed by theory and audience characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper concludes with considerations to be used in choosing the right medium for public relations messages (e.g., match medium to audience processing style, reach, and message complexity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case studies to bridge theory and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrate and test theoretical applications with case studies for each theory discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper presents case studies for general systems theory, social learning, social exchange, symmetrical communication, coorientation, and elaboration-likelihood theory to demonstrate practical writing and campaign decisions.
